name: Pale Rhodonite Pink
lede: Pale Rhodonite Pink is a soft purplish pink named for rhodonite, the rose-colored manganese mineral, and recorded by Robert Ridgway in 1912.

sections.title: A mineral's pale cousin
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 plate XXXVIII gives this hue as "pale rhodonite pink," one of several tones he built around the mineral name rhodonite [1]. The nearest named colors on file are [[baby-pink]] and [[pale-laelia-pink]], at Beyond the plate itself, who at Ridgway's office chose the modifier "pale" is undocumented here [1].

Rhodonite itself is a pink-to-red manganese silicate, first described from Russia's Ural Mountains in 1790, where it was carved into vases, columns and even an empress's sarcophagus [3]. The mineral's rose color comes from manganese ions, often cut through with dark, almost black veins of manganese oxide, which the pale, even swatch here does not show [3].

The ISCC-NBS 1955 revision of Ridgway's system calls this block 252, "pale purplish pink," measuring 4.0 units from the chip center in their system [1][2]. In LCH terms it sits at lightness 83, chroma 15, hue 13 degrees, close enough to [[baby-pink|Baby Pink]] to be mistaken for it at a glance, and only a little paler than [[queen-pink|Queen Pink]] [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds a screen match for this pink in only 6 of 23,781 paintings, as photographed, mostly nineteenth- and twentieth-century portraits and interiors [2]. That scarcity is typical of a pale, low-chroma tone: it blends into skin and fabric highlights rather than standing out as a named color [2]. The count is a computed color match, not a pigment identification, and every value here is a screen approximation of an aged printed plate [2].

questions.q: Pale Rhodonite Pink is named for what kind of thing?
True or false: raw rhodonite mineral looks like an even, pale pink with no markings.

openers: This pale pink is named for a mineral that's usually shot through with near-black veins — nothing like the smooth swatch here.
